summary.title: The Mathematical Hacker
summary.one_liner: Evan Miller argues that programmers, especially those doing practical work, should learn calculus, linear algebra and statistics, using closed-form Fibonacci and factorial examples in place of recursion.
takeaways: Many industries that once 'didn't need math' came to depend on it, and programmers can apply the same mathematical thinking to practical problems.
Closed-form solutions such as the Binet-style Fibonacci formula and the log-gamma factorial can replace recursion and run in constant time.
The author contrasts a 'Lisp school' focused on abstraction with a 'Fortran school' focused on applying mathematics to real-world problems.
Miller recommends that serious programmers study calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and numerical computing.
summary.summary: This 2012 opinion essay responds to views on math's relevance to programming from Eric Raymond, Paul Graham, and Steve Yegge. Miller argues that applied mathematics has driven much of twentieth-century industry and that programmers should know calculus, linear algebra, and statistics. He contrasts a Lisp-school focus on abstraction with a Fortran-school focus on mathematical problem solving. He illustrates the point with C code computing Fibonacci numbers analytically and factorials via log-gamma instead of recursion.
